analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan that negotiates prices directly with drug makers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, it sat on the Senate calendar until the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare's new prescription drug benefit started in 2006, it was delivered entirely through private insurance plans, and the law barred the government from negotiating drug prices. This bill would have required Medicare itself to offer a nationally available drug plan, negotiated prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, and charged seniors a uniform $35 monthly premium. It never received a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would get a government-run drug plan option with a uniform national premium set at $35 in 2006, alongside the existing private plans. The CRS summary states the plan would give enrollees 'access to negotiated prices,' and the bill directs the Secretary of HHS to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered drugs [S2] [S3]. Seniors who found private Part D plans confusing or costly would have a simpler, government-administered alternative with one national premium instead of a menu of regional plans [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans nationally, beginning in 2006, alongside the private plans created by the 2003 Medicare drug law [S2] [S3].

The Secretary would be required to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers over the purchase price of covered drugs and to encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents, using strategies similar to those of other federal drug purchasers [S2] [S3].
The monthly beneficiary premium would be uniform nationally — $35 in 2006, with the bill requiring at least one Medicare-operated plan at that premium [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face a federal purchaser negotiating prices instead of paying the prices set by private plans under the existing law's non-negotiation structure [S2] [S3]. Private insurers selling Part D plans would face a new government-run competitor. Federal taxpayers could bear some administrative cost of running the plan, and if negotiated prices plus the $35 premium did not cover actual costs, the difference would fall on the government [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Setting the 2006 premium by statute at $35 before any actual costs were known carried the risk that the premium would not cover the plan's real costs, leaving the difference to taxpayers or forcing later increases [S3].

A standard objection to government drug price negotiation is that lower prices reduce the revenue that funds pharmaceutical research and development, potentially slowing the development of new medicines; the bill does not address how its negotiation would weigh that tradeoff [S3].

The bill gives the Secretary discretion to designate the Medicare-operated plan as the government 'fallback' plan in any region, which critics of a public drug plan viewed as a step toward government displacement of private coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors — a cheaper, simpler, nationally uniform government drug plan with negotiated prices — is substantial and direct, and it existed at the time only as a private-market system widely criticized for complexity. The main costs are the fiscal risk of a statutorily fixed $35 premium and the disputed effect of price negotiation on pharmaceutical innovation. The design is a straightforward public-option addition rather than a sweeping restructuring: it leaves all private plans in place and adds one government alternative.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but with no committee referral, no cosponsors, and no floor action, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on April 21, 2005; it was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar the same day [S1] [S5].

The next day it was read a second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 90, but it was never referred to a committee, never marked up, and never brought to the floor [S3] [S5].
The bill had zero cosponsors throughout its life [S4].
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks in late September 2005, but no further legislative action followed [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died on the calendar without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurers who administer the Medicare drug benefit are better off: the existing structure of private-only Part D plans with no government negotiation survived intact, and no competitor plan was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor in September 2005.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership (109th Congress)
against.role: Senate majority, which controls the floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar under General Orders from April 2005 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split was never formally tested; it was a Democratic-sponsored proposal introduced while Republicans controlled the Senate and the White House.

industries.note: The bill requires the federal government to negotiate purchase prices directly with drug makers, replacing the non-negotiation structure of the 2003 drug law. Lower negotiated prices for Medicare's roughly 40 million beneficiaries would cut directly into drug company revenue on their largest customer.

industries.industry: Private Part D prescription drug insurers
industries.note: The bill adds a government-run plan competing directly with private insurers for the same enrollees, with a nationally uniform premium and federal negotiating power behind it. Insurers would keep their business under the bill, but face a lower-priced public competitor that could draw off enrollees.
